title: Data Types
summary: JavaScript values come in different kinds, and the kind affects what you can do with them.

subtopics.title: Text
subtopics.explanation: A string is text, commonly written inside quotes, such as `"hello"`. It is like a note containing words. String operations can join or inspect text, but do not assume a string that looks numeric is already a number. For example, convert an input value before adding it to a number; otherwise `+` may join text. In practice, convert a form string before calculating its numeric total.

subtopics.title: Numbers
subtopics.explanation: A number represents whole or decimal values. JavaScript uses one main number type for both. It is like a calculator reading. Check for invalid results and use intentional precision rules for financial values. For example, a score can be numeric while its formatted label is a string. In practice, keep a count as a number and format it as text only when displaying it.

subtopics.title: True or false
subtopics.explanation: A boolean is `true` or `false` and represents a yes-or-no state. It is like a switch. Use clear names such as `hasPermission` so the meaning of each state is obvious. For example, use a boolean to represent whether a user accepted a consent prompt. In practice, use a boolean to track whether a dialog is open.

subtopics.title: Missing values
subtopics.explanation: `undefined` often means a value was not provided; `null` often means an empty value was chosen intentionally. It is like a blank field that is either unanswered or deliberately cleared. Decide which meaning your app uses and check before calling methods on either value. For example, check both null and undefined if a value can be missing in either way. In practice, a missing property may evaluate to undefined even when the object exists.

subtopics.title: Objects
subtopics.explanation: An object groups related values under names, like a contact card with a name and phone number. Arrays are also objects in JavaScript. Objects can be nested and shared by reference, so changes may be visible through more than one variable. For example, a nested object may be shared by two variables that point to the same value. In practice, two variables can refer to the same object and observe one another’s mutations.

foundations.overview: JavaScript values have types that determine which operations make sense. Common types include strings, numbers, booleans, missing values, and objects. Think of them as different kinds of items in labeled containers. Knowing a value’s type helps prevent errors, but values from forms and servers still need checking before use.
foundations.whyItMatters: Knowing the value type clarifies which operations are safe and what checks are needed. It is especially useful when data moves between forms, APIs, and interface state.
foundations.mentalModel: JavaScript values have types that determine which operations make sense.
foundations.browserPerspective: The engine stores primitives directly (often on the stack or inline) and stores objects on the heap, with variables holding references (pointers) to them. Garbage collection reclaims objects once no references remain. typeof is resolved by the engine from the value's internal type tag.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Choosing number vs. bigint for large IDs, using null to represent 'no result' from an API, detecting arrays with Array.isArray, and copying objects carefully (spread/structuredClone) to avoid shared-reference bugs are everyday uses of type knowledge.
foundations.businessImpact: Type-related bugs (e.g., shared object mutations corrupting state, or precision loss with large numbers) can cause data corruption and customer-facing errors. Understanding types reduces such defects and the cost of fixing them.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Knowing value vs. reference semantics shapes how you copy data, pass arguments, and manage state (especially in frameworks like React where immutability matters). It also informs equality checks and defensive copying.
foundations.performanceImpact: Primitives are cheap to copy and compare; objects involve heap allocation and reference tracking. Excessive deep copying or holding references to large objects affects memory and speed, so understanding the model guides efficient choices.
commonUseCases: Choose a boolean for whether a dialog is open.
Keep a list of search results in an array and a record’s named fields in an object.
Distinguish missing input from an intentional empty value.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A string containing digits is already a number.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Text such as "12" must be converted and validated before numeric operations.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Null and undefined always mean exactly the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Applications often use them differently; agree on the meaning and check both when needed.

commonMisconceptions.myth: TypeScript or a variable name guarantees a runtime value’s type.
commonMisconceptions.reality: JavaScript values can arrive from forms or APIs and need runtime checks before use.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Objects always copy themselves when assigned to a new variable.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Assignment copies the reference, so both names may point to the same mutable object.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A boolean can represent several named statuses clearly.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Use a string union or another explicit model when the state has more than two choices.

visualExplorer.title: Value vs. reference: how JavaScript stores types
visualExplorer.caption: Step through what happens in memory when you copy a primitive versus an object.

config.intro: Follow two assignments — one primitive, one object — to see why one copy is independent and the other is shared.

steps.name: Declare a primitive
steps.detail: let a = 1 stores the value 1 directly in the variable a.

steps.name: Copy the primitive
steps.detail: let b = a copies the value; b is now an independent 1.

steps.name: Change the copy
steps.detail: b = 2 changes only b; a is still 1 because primitives are copied by value.

steps.name: Declare an object
steps.detail: const x = { v: 1 } creates the object on the heap; x holds a reference to it.

steps.name: Copy the reference
steps.detail: const y = x copies the reference, not the object — x and y point to the same object.

steps.name: Mutate through one
steps.detail: y.v = 2 changes the shared object, so x.v is also 2 — the surprise of reference types.

interactiveExamples.title: typeof across the types
interactiveExamples.explanation: typeof reveals each value's runtime type. Notice the two quirks: typeof null is 'object', and an array also reports 'object'.

sandbox.code:
console.log(typeof 'text');      // string
console.log(typeof 42);          // number
console.log(typeof true);        // boolean
console.log(typeof undefined);   // undefined
console.log(typeof null);        // object (quirk!)
console.log(typeof 10n);         // bigint
console.log(typeof Symbol());    // symbol
console.log(typeof [1, 2]);      // object
console.log(typeof function(){}); // function

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: string, number, boolean, undefined, object, bigint, symbol, object, function.

interactiveExamples.title: Primitives copy, objects share
interactiveExamples.explanation: Copying a primitive makes an independent value, but copying an object copies the reference — so changing one variable changes the other.

interactiveExamples.title: null vs. undefined
interactiveExamples.explanation: undefined is the default for unassigned variables; null is an intentional empty value. They are loosely equal but not strictly equal, and typeof treats them differently.

sandbox.code:
let notAssigned;
let empty = null;

console.log(notAssigned);            // undefined
console.log(empty);                  // null
console.log(typeof notAssigned);     // 'undefined'
console.log(typeof empty);           // 'object' (quirk)
console.log(notAssigned == empty);   // true (loose)
console.log(notAssigned === empty);  // false (strict)

codeLab.title: Write a robust type checker
codeLab.instructions: Implement typeName(value) that returns a clean type string: 'null' for null, 'array' for arrays, and otherwise the result of typeof. Test it on null, an array, a number, and a string.
hints: typeof null is 'object', so check value === null first.
Use Array.isArray to distinguish arrays from plain objects.

keyTakeaways: A string is text, commonly written inside quotes, such as `"hello"`.
A number represents whole or decimal values.
A boolean is `true` or `false` and represents a yes-or-no state.
`undefined` often means a value was not provided; `null` often means an empty value was chosen intentionally.
An object groups related values under names, like a contact card with a name and phone number.
